analysis.one_liner: Restricts when federal police can use force and pushes states to adopt the same rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: 84 House Democrats backed it, but it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a matter of law, not just policy, that federal officers may use deadly force only as a last resort to stop an imminent threat of death or serious injury, and less lethal force only when necessary and proportionate after trying other options. It would require officers to identify themselves and warn people before using force, require special guidance for encounters with children, pregnant women, the elderly, people with disabilities, and others, and narrow the legal defense available to federal officers charged with murder or manslaughter. To get states to follow, it would cut off Edward Byrne Memorial grant money to any state whose use-of-force law doesn't meet the same standard, while offering grants directly to local governments within those states that adopt compliant policies.
analysis.who_benefits: People who encounter law enforcement — especially people of color, people with disabilities, people in mental health crises, children, and the elderly — gain enforceable limits on when officers may use force against them, and families of people killed by officers gain a narrower legal defense to overcome. Taxpayers also gain from federal grant dollars being tied to a use-of-force standard instead of being unconditional.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in encounters with police, especially vulnerable groups

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal officers from using deadly force except as a last resort to prevent imminent death or serious bodily injury, and requires that no bystander face substantial risk of injury and that all reasonable alternatives have been exhausted first [S3].
Bars less lethal force unless it is necessary, proportionate, and used only after reasonable alternatives — verbal warnings, creating distance, de-escalation — have been tried [S3].
Requires officers to identify themselves and give a verbal warning to surrender before using force when feasible [S3].

Directs the Attorney General to issue guidance and training on force used against pregnant women, children, elderly people, people with disabilities, people impaired by drugs or medical conditions, and people with limited English [S3].

Limits the justification defense for federal officers charged with murder or manslaughter when their force violated the new standard or when their own gross negligence created the need for force [S3].

Withholds Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds from states lacking a consistent use-of-force law, while allowing local governments in those states to still receive equivalent grants if their own police agencies adopt compliant policies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies and state and local police departments bear the cost of retraining, revised policies, and new accountability standards; states that refuse to adopt the standard lose federal justice grant money, which could reduce funding for local crime programs in those states.

drawbacks.text: The Deadly-force standard is stricter than the constitutional rule courts apply today, and police organizations argue a 'last resort' standard puts officers and the public at risk in fast-moving, ambiguous encounters — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh [S3].
Withholding Byrne grant funds could cut money for local crime prevention and drug task forces in states that decline to change their laws, hurting the residents the bill aims to protect [S3].

The restriction on the justification defense applies only to federal officers, and state-level compliance hinges on Attorney General discretion to judge whether state laws are 'consistent,' leaving room for uneven enforcement across administrations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is enforceable restraint on lethal force against stronger legal accountability for officers, paid for by retraining costs and possible losses of federal grant money in non-compliant states. The federal-only pieces are narrow in scope; the state-level piece is where the impact on everyday policing would be felt, but it depends entirely on grant-condition enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill in the House on September 17, 2019, joined by 84 Democratic cosponsors [S1, S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and two weeks later to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police unions and law enforcement agencies that would have faced the new use-of-force limits and grant conditions are better off, because the bill never moved; so are states that would have refused the conditions and lost Byrne grant funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies and resistant states

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 84 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee and then in the Crime Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Law enforcement associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed use-of-force restriction bills of this kind during the period; the bill itself contemplated consulting them on guidance.

sides.party_line_note: All 84 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the bill advanced no further in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: The bill would impose binding use-of-force limits, mandatory warning and de-escalation practices, retraining, and criminal exposure when officers' own negligence creates the need for force. Its benefit to the public is the constraint on agencies themselves.

The narrower justification defense and the 'necessary force only' standard would strengthen the legal position of people suing or charging officers, the outcome unions opposed during the 2020 policing debates.

industries.industry: State and local governments reliant on Byrne JAG grants
industries.note: Compliant states keep full grant funding and gain a direct pathway for local grants; states that refuse would lose Byrne funds, though the bill lets local governments within them recoup equivalent money by adopting compliant policies.
